whyCorrect: The goal is narrow: contrast the orbits of the two moons. Only the two orbital-period bullets do that work — Miranda takes 1.41 Earth days, Oberon takes 13.46 — so the answer has to set those two numbers against each other, and it has to stay true to the notes. Saying Miranda orbits many times faster than Oberon does exactly that: it is a direct comparison of the two moons' orbits, and it is what the numbers show (13.46 is roughly ten times 1.41). Every other choice either drops the contrast or adds a claim the notes do not support.

whyWrong.B: This is about Kepler's laws applying to moons, not about how the two orbits differ; it groups Oberon and Miranda together instead of contrasting them.
whyWrong.C: It looks like the most detailed contrast, which is the trap, but it contradicts the notes: the notes say Kepler's laws apply to the elliptical orbits of natural satellites, so calling Miranda's orbit circular is a fact the notes do not support.
whyWrong.D: This compares the moons to planets, not Miranda to Oberon, so it accomplishes a different goal than the one stated.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option with the most numbers in it. On a notes question, accuracy comes first — a detailed sentence that misstates one bullet is still wrong.
tips: Read the sentence after the bullets first. It names the goal, and any choice that does something else is out before you weigh the details.

whyCorrect: The proposal has two moving parts: high metabolism is an advantage in a mass extinction, and birds had more of it than non-avian dinosaurs did, so birds are the ones that lived. To undermine it you need a case where a high metabolic rate did not come with survival. That is exactly what D supplies — many creatures with very high metabolic rates died in the same event — which breaks the link between the rate and the outcome the proposal depends on.

whyWrong.A: If non-avian dinosaurs' metabolisms fell over time, they entered the extinction with lower rates than birds, which strengthens the proposal rather than undermining it.
whyWrong.B: This points in the right direction but stops short: it only makes high rates in some non-avian dinosaurs likely, and it never states that a high-rate animal failed to survive, so it leaves the proposal standing.
whyWrong.C: This says birds have very high metabolisms, which is the premise the proposal is built on; it supports the argument instead of weakening it.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice that talks about metabolism without asking which direction it pushes. Undermine questions turn on the direction of the evidence, not the topic.
tips: State the proposal as an if-then before you read the choices — here, 'if high metabolism, then survived' — and then hunt for the choice that supplies a counterexample.

whyCorrect: Track what the text actually does, sentence by sentence: it names the Museum of Latin American Art, says what it is dedicated to, then names the National Hispanic Cultural Center and says what it focuses on. Two institutions, and for each one a statement of its subject matter — that is the whole shape of the passage. C describes that shape without adding anything the text does not do.

whyWrong.A: Funding never comes up. The text mentions that the museum has acquired more than 1,300 objects, but it says nothing about where the money came from.
whyWrong.B: A collection size is given for only one of the two institutions, so the text cannot be drawing a contrast between their sizes.
whyWrong.D: No historical development is traced. Founding dates and locations are given, but nothing in the text explains what led to either institution being founded.

commonMistakes: Latching onto the 1,300-objects detail and assuming the passage must be about collections. One supporting detail does not set the purpose of the whole text.
tips: For a main-purpose question, check the choice against every sentence. If a choice only covers half the passage, or covers something the passage never says, it is out.

whyCorrect: Compare the two halves. Before the blank, an information cascade helps the group — the fish copy a real escape and survive. After it, the same copying spreads misinformation and hurts the group: sandpipers abandon safe nesting grounds over false alarms. Same mechanism, opposite outcome, so the blank needs a transition that flips the direction, and conversely is the only one that does.

whyWrong.A: In other words announces a restatement, but the sandpiper study is not a rephrasing of the fish study — it reports the opposite result.
whyWrong.C: Indeed intensifies or confirms the point just made, which would require the second sentence to add more evidence that cascades benefit the collective. It does the reverse.
whyWrong.D: Consequently claims the second sentence follows as an effect of the first. Fish escaping a predator successfully does not cause sandpipers to flee false alarms; these are two independent studies.

commonMistakes: Reading only the sentence before the blank. A transition is decided by the relationship between the two sides, so you have to read past the blank to the end.
tips: Label each half with a plus or a minus first. Here it is benefit, then harm — a sign change means you want a contrast word.

whyCorrect: The notes give you the one point of difference: Fodor calls low-level systems modular but says high-level systems are not, while Carruthers's MMH extends modularity to all cognitive systems. So the comparison is about scope — MMH covers everything, Fodor covers only part. B states precisely that, and it is the only choice that puts both hypotheses side by side and says how they differ.

whyWrong.A: It misreads the disagreement. Carruthers did not reject the idea that the mind contains innate modules; he accepted it and widened it, so this states a conflict the notes do not describe.
whyWrong.C: The two men agree about low-level systems — both call perception and language modular. The difference is over high-level systems such as reasoning, so this names the wrong point of difference.
whyWrong.D: This reports the order in which the two hypotheses appeared and then describes only Carruthers's. It never says what Fodor held, so no comparison is made.

commonMistakes: Treating any sentence that names both scientists as a comparison. A comparison has to state a specific point on which the two positions line up or diverge.
tips: Write the difference in your own words from the notes before reading the choices — here, 'Fodor: some systems; Carruthers: all systems' — then find the choice that matches it.
